title: A Structure Is a Building: Design It From the Loads, Then Draw It Twice
summary: A legal and tax structure should be designed the way an engineer designs a building: start from the loads it must carry, draw how money flows and how control flows, and decide the order in which the pieces are built. This lesson introduces the six lenses as design loads, the two diagrams every structure needs, and why sequencing is part of the design.
body:
A structure is not a set of companies you collect. It is a design that must carry six loads at once, drawn twice, once for money and once for control, and built in the right order, because a piece put in place too late can cost more than the whole structure saves.

Recall

Q. What is a time bar in a construction contract?

A. A clause that extinguishes a claim if written notice is not given within a set period. How strictly courts enforce it varies by jurisdiction.

Q. What is a job hazard analysis?

A. A written breakdown of a task into steps, the hazards in each step and the controls for each hazard, prepared before the work starts and reviewed with the crew.

Q. What is the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR)?

A. Net operating income divided by annual debt service. A lender sets a minimum as a commercial term, not a standard, and sizes the loan so the project clears it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this phase is about cross-border structure and tax strategy. Most developers meet structure backwards. They form a company because an accountant said so, buy land in whatever name is handy, add a holding company when an investor asks, and discover years later that the structure taxes them twice, gives a lender no clean security, or cannot be sold without a large tax bill. A structure built that way is like a building designed floor by floor as the money arrives. It may stand. It will not stand well.

The alternative is to design first. That does not mean complexity. The best structure is usually the simplest one that carries every load. This week teaches the method; the rest of the phase fills in residence, treaties, repatriation, financing, transfer pricing, indirect tax, moving money and exit.

The six lenses are the design loads

In plain English: every structure is pushed on by six forces, and a design that ignores one fails along that line.

The professional framing is the six lenses this course has used since Week 27. Tax: what each layer pays and what leaks as money moves. Liability: which assets a claim can reach. Banking: whether a lender can take clean security and whether accounts can be opened and run. Governance: who decides, who signs and how disputes are settled. Estate: what happens on death or incapacity. Exit: how the asset or the business can be sold, refinanced or passed on. A structure chart that answers all six is designed. One that answers two is a tax plan with five other problems attached.

A worked example, hypothetical. You plan one apartment building with a partner. Option A: you both own the land personally, as co-owners. Option B: a single project company owns the land, and each of you owns shares in it through your own holding company. Under liability, Option A exposes both your personal estates to the project; Option B ring-fences the project. Under banking, a lender in Option B takes security over one company's assets and shares, which is cleaner. Under estate, in Option A each owner's death puts a share of the land into probate; in Option B only shares move. Under exit, Option B lets you sell the company or the building. Tax could favour either, depending on local rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Option B costs more to run. Whether it is worth it is now a decision, not an accident.

Draw it twice: funds and control

Every structure needs two diagrams. The flow-of-funds diagram shows where money enters, every place it is taxed or charged, and where it finally lands. The flow-of-control diagram shows who appoints directors, who signs, who can veto and who can remove whom. The two often differ, and the difference is where trouble lives. A company can receive the money while a shareholder agreement gives control to someone else; a trust can hold the shares while a protector holds the power to replace the trustee.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Rent of 1,000,000 dollars a year arrives in the project company. It pays operating costs and interest, leaving taxable profit. After tax in the project company, it pays a dividend to two holding companies, each of which may pay further tax or withholding before money reaches you. Draw each arrow with its label: rent, interest, tax, dividend, withholding. Now draw control: the project company's board has two directors, one appointed by each holding company, with a deadlock clause in the shareholder agreement. If the funds diagram and the control diagram cannot both fit on one page, the structure is too complicated for you to run.

Say that out loud now.

Draw the money, draw the control, and if both do not fit on one page, simplify.

Sequencing: the order is part of the design

A structure is built in time, and the order matters as much as the shape. Land signed in your personal name and later moved into a company can trigger transfer tax twice and a taxable disposition on the move. An investor admitted before the shareholder agreement is signed may be admitted on terms you never chose. A bank account opened before the company's signing authority is resolved is opened on the wrong mandate. Sequencing means writing down, before anything happens, which entity exists first, which contract is signed in which name, and which approvals come before money moves. The principle is general; the tax effects are local, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

How the best do it

Well-run development groups keep a single structure memorandum for every project: one page of diagrams, one page explaining each entity's purpose in a sentence, and a short sequencing plan. It is updated whenever the structure changes and is sent to the lender, the auditors and the tax advisers together, so that each adviser sees the whole design rather than the piece they were paid to review. A small developer can copy this exactly. The memo costs a few hours and saves the most expensive conversation in development: the one where two advisers discover that their separate advice does not fit together.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: every layer is a place money can be taxed again, so each must earn its place. Liability: separate companies ring-fence risk only if they are run as separate, with their own records and accounts. Banking: a lender wants to see the whole chart and the security it can take before it lends. Governance: the control diagram should name who signs and who decides, and match the minute books. Estate: shares in a holding company are easier to pass on than land, but only if your estate plan knows they exist. Exit: design the exit before the entry; a structure that cannot be sold cleanly is a structure that traps value.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser and corporate lawyer, in each jurisdiction the structure touches, reviewing the same memorandum.

Start from the simplest design

Before adding anything, write down the simplest structure that could work: one project company owning the land and the loan. Test it against each of the six lenses and note where it fails. Only add a layer to fix a named failure. A worked example: the single company fails the estate lens because your share would pass through probate in a country where you do not live. A holding company in your country of residence may fix that. Now you know why the holding company exists, and you can test whether it creates a new failure elsewhere, for example a withholding cost the single company did not have.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure assembled one adviser at a time, each solving one lens, with nobody responsible for the whole. The control is a single structure memorandum owned by you, reviewed by every adviser together, and updated before any change is made.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner adds entities because each one sounds protective. Every entity adds cost, filings, bank accounts, audit risk and places for money to leak. If you cannot state an entity's purpose in one sentence, it probably should not exist.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught minute books, resolutions and signing authority. The control diagram is those records drawn as a picture. If the picture and the minute book disagree, the minute book is what a court, a lender or a tax authority will read.

Recap

Design a structure from six loads: tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit. Draw the flow of funds and the flow of control on one page each. Sequence the build so entities, agreements and authorities exist before money and land move. Keep one structure memorandum that every adviser reads.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Enron, and what happens when structure is designed to hide rather than to carry.
checklist: I can name the six lenses and what each asks of a structure.
I have a flow-of-funds diagram with every tax and charge labelled.
I have a flow-of-control diagram showing who appoints, signs and vetoes.
Both diagrams fit on one page each.
I can state each entity's purpose in one sentence.
I have written a sequencing plan before land or money moves.
Every adviser reviews the same structure memorandum.
My control diagram matches the minute books.
head: Field checklist
speak: A structure is a design, not a collection of companies. It must carry six loads at once: tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit. I draw it twice. The flow-of-funds diagram shows where money enters, every place it is taxed or charged, and where it lands. The flow-of-control diagram shows who appoints directors, who signs and who can veto. Where the two differ is where trouble lives, and if they do not each fit on one page, the structure is too complicated to run. Then I sequence it: which entity exists first, which contract is signed in which name, and which approvals come before money moves, because land signed in the wrong name can be taxed twice when it is moved. I keep one structure memorandum, with diagrams, a one-sentence purpose for each entity and the sequencing plan, and every adviser reviews the same document. The simplest structure that carries every load wins.
terms: Flow-of-funds diagram — a drawing of where money enters a structure, where it is taxed or charged, and where it lands.
Flow-of-control diagram — a drawing of who appoints, signs, decides and can veto in each entity.
Sequencing — the planned order in which entities are formed, contracts signed and money moved.

hostile.q: Why do you need four entities to own one apartment building?
hostile.a: I may not, and the structure memorandum is where I test that. Each entity has a one-sentence purpose: the project company holds the land and the loan so you get clean security; each holding company holds one partner's shares so a partner's own affairs do not touch the project. If an entity cannot state its purpose against the six lenses, it goes. I will show you the funds diagram, the control diagram and the security you take in each.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (audit and integrity) assisting
title: Enron 2001: Structure Built to Hide Rather Than to Carry
summary: Enron filed for bankruptcy in December 2001 after it emerged that off-balance-sheet entities, some run by its own finance chief, had kept debt and losses out of view. The failure was not that Enron used many entities; it was that the structure was designed so outsiders could not see the risk it carried. A developer's structure must survive being drawn in full for a lender.
body:
Enron filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001. Its structure was built not to carry risk safely but to move risk out of sight, and once outsiders could see it, confidence and the company vanished within weeks.

Recall

Q. What are the two diagrams every structure needs?

A. A flow-of-funds diagram, showing where money enters, is taxed or charged and lands, and a flow-of-control diagram, showing who appoints, signs and vetoes.

Q. What is a site-specific safety plan?

A. A written plan for one project setting out its hazards, controls, responsibilities, training and emergency procedures, required before work starts.

Q. What does the in-balance test compare?

A. Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity against the full cost to complete. If the funds fall short, the borrower deposits the gap before the next draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is an audit and integrity case. Enron was an energy and trading company, not a developer, but its failure is the clearest public example of structure used as camouflage. The broad facts here come from the company's own restatements, the bankruptcy, the board's special investigative report and later criminal trials. I keep to them and avoid figures I cannot confirm.

1. Timeline

Through the 1990s Enron grew from a pipeline company into a large energy trader and presented itself as a model of new business. It used many special purpose entities, separate companies or partnerships formed for a narrow purpose, some of which kept assets and debt off its balance sheet. Several were run by its chief financial officer, Andrew Fastow, while he remained in that role. In August 2001 the chief executive, Jeffrey Skilling, resigned. In October 2001 Enron announced a large loss and a reduction in shareholders' equity linked to these entities. In November 2001 it restated several years of results. On 2 December 2001 it filed for bankruptcy protection. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, was convicted of obstruction in 2002, a conviction the United States Supreme Court overturned in 2005, by which time the firm had largely collapsed. Several executives, including Fastow and Skilling, were later convicted.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions carried the outcome. Using entities whose purpose was to keep debt and losses off the main balance sheet. Allowing the finance chief to run and profit from entities that dealt with the company he served; the board waived its own conflict-of-interest rules to allow it. And supporting some of those entities with Enron's own shares, so that their protection depended on Enron's share price staying high.

3. Assumptions

The structure assumed the share price would keep rising, that accounting treatment would hold under scrutiny, and that counterparties and rating agencies would keep lending on the reported numbers. Each assumption depended on the others. When the share price fell, the entities' protection weakened, losses came back onto the balance sheet, and the reported numbers stopped being believed.

4. Incentives

Reported earnings drove the share price, the share price drove executive pay and the company's ability to borrow, and the entities protected reported earnings. The executive running the entities was paid by both sides. Advisers were paid well for structuring work. Very few people in the chain were paid to say that the structure, drawn in full, did not make sense.

Say that out loud now.

If the structure only works while nobody can see it, it does not work.

5. Warning signs ignored

The disclosures about related-party transactions were long and hard to understand; outsiders who tried to read them often could not. The conflict waiver itself was a warning: a board allowing its finance chief to sit on both sides of transactions. Returns reported from trading were difficult to reconcile with cash generated. Some analysts and journalists asked publicly how the company made its money. Each warning was answered with confidence rather than with a clear diagram.

6. Point of no return

Once the company announced the loss and equity reduction in October 2001, trust collapsed faster than any balance sheet could be repaired. A trading company lives on credit from its counterparties, and they withdrew it. The point of no return was earlier, though: the moment the structure depended on the share price it was designed to support.

7. Root cause

Cole's finding: the structure was designed for presentation, not for carrying risk, and governance allowed the person designing it to profit from it. No independent party had to sign a full flow-of-funds and flow-of-control picture of the group that an outsider could understand. Entities, in themselves, did nothing wrong. Their purpose did.

The developer's translation

A worked example, hypothetical. You propose a land-holding company owned by you personally that leases a site to your project company, in which investors hold 60 percent. The lease rent is set by you, on both sides. To an investor or lender this is a related-party transaction: you profit from the land company at the project company's expense. It may be perfectly fair. The control is to disclose it on the structure chart, set the rent by an independent valuation, and have the investors approve it. If you would rather they did not notice, you have answered the question.

A second example. A lender asks for your full structure chart before term sheet. You hesitate because one entity holds a personal guarantee you would rather not discuss. Show it anyway. A lender that finds an undisclosed liability after closing will treat every other statement you made as doubtful, and an undisclosed fact can also be a misrepresentation; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Cole's three questions for any entity

Cole's note. Ask of every entity: what does it carry that could not be carried elsewhere, who controls it and is that person also on the other side of its transactions, and what would a lender or investor see if it were drawn in full. A good entity answers all three in a sentence each. An entity that answers "it improves how the numbers look" has failed the first question already.

What the board report found

After the collapse, a special committee of Enron's board commissioned an investigation, widely known by the name of its chair, William Powers. Its report criticised the related-party partnerships, the accounting judgments behind them and the oversight the board itself had provided. The point for you is not the detail of any one transaction. It is that a board can approve every individual step and still fail, because nobody was asked to look at the whole picture and say whether it made sense.

That is the job of a structure memorandum on a small scale. Each entity, each related-party fee and each guarantee may be reasonable alone. Drawn together on one page, the combination either tells an honest story about where risk sits or it does not. Read the page as an outsider would, every time it changes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure whose value depends on outsiders not understanding it. The control is a one-page structure chart, with every related-party arrangement disclosed, shown to lenders and investors before they commit.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that something lawful by an adviser's opinion must be safe. Advice addresses the question asked. Whether a structure can survive being seen in full is a question you must ask yourself.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught substance over form: authorities and courts can look through the legal shape to what is really happening. Enron's entities had legal form and little substance apart from presentation. When the form stopped being believed, the substance was all that remained.

Recap

Enron used entities, some run by its own finance chief, to keep debt and losses off its balance sheet, supported by its own share price. When the price fell, the structure unwound, trust went and the company filed for bankruptcy in December 2001. Rule 55: every entity has a one-sentence business purpose, every related-party arrangement is disclosed, and the full structure is drawn on one page for any lender or investor before they commit.

Next: Warrick, on The Money: what each layer of a structure costs and where money leaks on its way home.
checklist: Every entity in my structure has a one-sentence business purpose.
I disclose every related-party arrangement on the structure chart.
Related-party prices are set by independent evidence and approved by the other owners.
No entity's protection depends on the value of the thing it protects.
I show my full structure chart to lenders and investors before they commit.
No one controls both sides of an intercompany transaction without independent approval.
I ask whether my structure would survive being drawn in full by a sceptic.
head: Field checklist
speak: Enron filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001. It used special purpose entities to keep debt and losses off its balance sheet, some run by its own chief financial officer while he served, with the board waiving its conflict rules to allow it. Some of those entities were supported by Enron's own shares, so their protection depended on the share price staying high. When the price fell, losses returned to the balance sheet, the company announced a large loss, restated years of results, and counterparties withdrew credit. The root cause was a structure designed to present rather than to carry risk, with governance that let its designer profit from it. Entities did nothing wrong; their purpose did. My rule is Rule 55: every entity has a one-sentence business purpose, every related-party arrangement is disclosed, and the full structure fits on one page shown to any lender or investor before they commit.
terms: Special purpose entity — a company or partnership formed for one narrow purpose, such as holding an asset or a loan.
Related-party transaction — a deal between parties under common control or influence, such as a company and its owner's other company.
Off-balance-sheet — assets or debts held outside a company's reported balance sheet, often in a separate entity.

hostile.q: Your land company leases the site to the project company, and you own the land company outright. Why should investors accept that?
hostile.a: Because it is disclosed, priced independently and approved by you. The land company exists so that the land, which I contribute, stays separate from construction risk. The rent was set by an independent appraisal, it is shown on the structure chart, and the shareholder agreement makes any change to it a major decision needing your approval. If you would prefer, the project company can hold an option to buy the land at appraised value.

rule: Rule 55: Every entity in my structure has a business purpose I can state in one sentence, every related-party arrangement is disclosed and independently priced, and the whole structure is drawn on one page and shown to any lender or investor before they commit.

title: What Every Layer Costs: Leakage on the Way Home
summary: Each entity between a building and its owner can add tax, withholding, fees and running costs, and the total of these is called leakage. This lesson shows how to measure leakage across a structure in one table, how to weigh it against what each layer protects, and what it means for a personal balance sheet.
body:
Money earned in a building has to travel home, and every layer it passes through can take a toll. Measure the tolls in one table, and keep a layer only when what it protects is worth more than what it costs.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 55?

A. Every entity has a one-sentence business purpose, every related-party arrangement is disclosed and independently priced, and the whole structure is drawn on one page for any lender or investor before they commit.

Q. Name the four Focus Four hazards.

A. Falls, struck-by, caught-in or caught-between, and electrocution.

Q. What is the difference between senior debt and mezzanine debt?

A. Senior debt is repaid first and is usually secured on the property. Mezzanine debt sits below it, is often secured on the shares of the borrower, and is paid only after senior debt, so it costs more.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, developers talk about project returns. Wealth builders care about what arrives in their own hands after every layer has taken its share. The gap can be large, and it is often invisible until the first distribution. This lesson gives you the table that makes it visible before you build the structure.

The four kinds of leakage

In plain English: money can be lost on the way home to tax, to withholding, to fees and to the cost of running the entities themselves.

The professional framing. Income tax at the project level, on profit. Withholding tax, which a country may charge when money is paid out to a non-resident, for example on dividends or interest; treaties may reduce it, a subject for Week 57. Tax at each holding layer, which may or may not apply depending on local rules for intercompany dividends. And friction: accounting, audit, legal filings, bank fees, registered agents and directors' fees for every entity, every year. All rates and rules here are hypothetical; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Measuring it in one table

A worked example with hypothetical round numbers and hypothetical rates, chosen only to show the method. A project company earns 1,000,000 dollars of taxable profit. Assume project-level tax of 25 percent, leaving 750,000 dollars. It pays all of that as a dividend to a foreign holding company. Assume withholding of 10 percent on the dividend, so 75,000 dollars is withheld and 675,000 dollars arrives. Assume the holding company pays no further tax on that dividend but costs 40,000 dollars a year to run. It then pays 635,000 dollars to you, and assume you pay personal tax of 20 percent on it, 127,000 dollars, leaving 508,000 dollars.

StepTollRemaining
Project profit01,000,000
Project tax, hypothetical 25 percent250,000750,000
Withholding, hypothetical 10 percent75,000675,000
Holding company running cost40,000635,000
Personal tax, hypothetical 20 percent127,000508,000

Total leakage is 492,000 dollars, or about 49 percent of project profit. The useful question is not "is 49 percent high?" but "which line can I change, and what does the change cost me in protection?"

Say that out loud now.

Leakage is tax, withholding, holding-layer tax and friction; I measure all four in one table before I build the structure.

Weighing a layer

A second worked example. Suppose removing the holding company would save its 40,000 dollars of running cost but, under the hypothetical rules of this example, raise withholding to 15 percent because you would receive the dividend directly. Withholding becomes 112,500 dollars instead of 75,000, an extra 37,500 dollars. The saving is only 2,500 dollars a year, and you lose the holding company's other benefits: a single place to collect income from several projects, a cleaner sale of shares, and a buffer between the project and your personal estate. On those numbers the layer earns its keep. Change the assumptions and the answer may flip; that is why the table is rebuilt for each structure and checked by a tax adviser.

Two further costs hide outside the table. Timing: money held in a layer and not yet paid home may be taxed later, which is a deferral, worth money because tax paid later costs less in today's value. And trapped cash: money that cannot leave a layer without a large toll is not really yours to spend. A structure that looks efficient on annual leakage can still trap cash at exit, the subject of Week 64.

Friction is a fixed cost, so scale matters

Running costs barely change with the size of the project. A holding company costing 40,000 dollars a year is 4 percent of 1,000,000 dollars of profit but 0.4 percent of 10,000,000 dollars. On a small first project the same structure that suits a large portfolio may be heavy. Many developers start simple and add layers when the portfolio can carry them, which is a sequencing decision, not a failure to plan, provided the later move is planned so it does not itself trigger tax; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. On your personal balance sheet, value a share in a project at what would reach you after leakage, not at your share of project value. If a building is worth 10,000,000 dollars of equity to the project company and a sale would lose a third on the way home, your personal asset is closer to 6,700,000 dollars than 10,000,000. Plan your liquidity floor and your spending from the after-leakage figure. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

A worked check on friction

List every running cost for each entity, hypothetical figures. Annual accounts and audit, 15,000 dollars. Tax returns in one or two countries, 8,000 dollars. Registered office and corporate secretary, 4,000 dollars. Local directors' fees, 10,000 dollars. Bank fees and compliance reviews, 3,000 dollars. Total 40,000 dollars a year, the figure used above. Over a ten-year hold, that is 400,000 dollars before any inflation in fees. Now add the one-off costs: formation, legal opinions and the cost of eventually winding the entity up. A layer that saves 30,000 dollars a year in tax looks attractive until you put 400,000 dollars of friction beside it over ten years. Count both, over the same period.

Friction also has a non-money cost: your attention. Every entity is another set of deadlines, another signature you must give and another place where a missed filing triggers a penalty. If your days already run on a rotating shift, that time is scarce. A structure you cannot keep current is not a structure you should build.

A last check before you build: ask who will notice if a layer stops being worth it. Tax rules change, treaties are renegotiated and your portfolio grows or shrinks. Put a date in your calendar each year to rebuild the leakage table with current rates and running costs. A layer that earned its place five years ago may now cost more than it saves, and removing it carefully is as much a design decision as adding it was.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring leakage on one year's income while ignoring what the structure costs at sale or on death. The control is to build the leakage table three times: for annual income, for a sale and for a death, before you commit to the structure.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner chooses a structure to minimise one tax line and ignores friction and trapped cash. A structure that saves 20,000 dollars of tax and costs 50,000 dollars to run is a loss with a good story.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage and Elias introduced after-tax leakage in returns. Today's table is that idea applied to a structure: the project's internal rate of return is the building's performance, and what reaches you after every layer is yours.

Recap

Leakage has four parts: project tax, withholding, holding-layer tax and friction. Measure them in one table, test each layer by what it saves against what it protects, and build the table for income, sale and death. Value your personal holdings after leakage.

Next: Omar, on The Rules: the laws that test a structure, from separate legal personality to anti-avoidance rules, with a comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: I can name the four kinds of leakage.
I have a leakage table for annual income through my structure.
I have rebuilt the table for a sale and for a death.
I can state what each layer protects against what it costs.
I know each entity's annual running cost.
I value my personal holdings after leakage, not at project value.
A tax adviser has checked every rate in my table against primary sources.
head: Field checklist
speak: Money earned in a building travels home through every layer of a structure, and each layer can take a toll. There are four kinds of leakage: tax at the project level, withholding when money is paid to a non-resident, tax at any holding layer, and friction, the yearly cost of running each entity. I measure them in one table. In a hypothetical example, 1 million dollars of project profit loses a quarter to project tax, a tenth of the dividend to withholding, 40 thousand to the holding company and a fifth to personal tax, leaving about 508 thousand. Then I test each layer: what does removing it save, and what protection does it cost? Friction is fixed, so a layer that suits a portfolio may be heavy for one project. I build the table for income, for a sale and for a death, and I value my own holdings after leakage, never at project value.
terms: Leakage — the total of tax, withholding and running costs lost as money moves from a project to its ultimate owner.
Withholding tax — tax a country may deduct when income is paid to a non-resident, such as on dividends or interest.
Deferral — postponing tax to a later date, which has value because tax paid later costs less in today's money.

hostile.q: Your structure loses almost half the profit before it reaches you. Why not simplify it?
hostile.a: I may, and the leakage table tells me what simplifying costs. Removing the holding company saves 40 thousand a year but, on these assumptions, raises withholding by 37,500 and removes the buffer between the project and my estate and the clean share sale at exit. On those numbers the layer earns its place. I have also run the table for a sale and for a death, and a tax adviser has checked every rate. If the assumptions change, so will the structure.

title: The Law That Tests a Structure: Personality, Substance and Anti-Avoidance
summary: A structure rests on the rule that a company is a separate legal person, and it is tested by doctrines that look through form to substance: veil piercing, sham and anti-avoidance rules. This lesson explains those concepts, how they are applied, and, in Two Systems, how Canada and Guyana approach the point in general terms.
body:
The law gives you separate companies, and the law can look through them. A structure is safe only when its legal form and its real substance tell the same story.

Recall

Q. What are the four kinds of leakage in a structure?

A. Project-level tax, withholding tax on payments to non-residents, tax at holding layers, and friction, meaning the yearly cost of running each entity.

Q. What does a GMP not cover?

A. Owner changes, allowances that run over, escalation outside agreed bands, excluded work and risks the contract leaves with the owner.

Q. What is an intercreditor agreement?

A. An agreement between lenders at different levels of the capital stack setting priority of payment, cure rights and limits on enforcement.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every structure you build relies on a promise from the law: that a company is a person separate from its owners. Every tax authority and every unpaid creditor has tools to test that promise. These are concepts, not conclusions for any jurisdiction. The rules differ by country and change over time; verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it, and have local counsel confirm it.

Separate legal personality

In plain English: a company owns its own assets, owes its own debts and signs its own contracts, and its shareholders are not personally liable for those debts beyond what they invested or guaranteed.

The professional framing is separate legal personality, with limited liability as its usual consequence. It is the foundation of ring-fencing: a project company that fails should take only its own assets with it. But personality is a legal status that must be maintained. A company with its own bank account, its own minutes, its own contracts and arm's-length dealings with its owners looks like a separate person. One whose money is mixed with its owner's, whose decisions are never minuted and whose contracts are signed in the owner's name looks like a mask.

Looking through the form

Three families of doctrine let a court or authority look through. Veil piercing, taught in Week 21, lets a court hold owners liable for a company's obligations in narrow cases, typically where the company was used to evade an existing obligation or was a mere façade. Sham: a document that does not reflect what the parties really agreed may be disregarded. And in tax, substance over form and anti-avoidance rules: authorities may recharacterise a transaction by what it really does, and many countries have a general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR), a broad statutory power to deny a tax benefit from arrangements whose main purpose is avoiding tax and which abuse the purpose of the law. Tests differ widely; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. You form a company in another country to own your project shares, with the aim of a lower withholding rate. Its only director is a local nominee who signs whatever you send. It has no office, no staff and no decisions of its own; all money passes straight through to you within a day. An authority asking what this entity really does may conclude it does nothing but route money, and deny the benefit under an anti-avoidance rule or a treaty's anti-abuse provisions. The form said holding company. The substance said conduit.

Say that out loud now.

Form gives me separate companies; substance decides whether the law will respect them.

Related-party rules

Most tax systems also have specific rules for dealings between connected parties: rules requiring arm's-length prices, limits on interest deductions for related-party debt, and reporting duties. These are narrower than a GAAR and often more mechanical. Weeks 60 and 61 take thin capitalisation and transfer pricing in depth. For now, the design principle is that any payment between your own entities must be one you could defend as fair if a stranger had been on the other side.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your management company charges your project company a fee of 8 percent of construction cost. Independent project managers in your market charge 3 to 4 percent for the same scope. An authority may treat the excess as a disguised distribution, deny part of the deduction, or both. The fix is to set the fee by evidence of market rates and document the services actually performed.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach the point. Verify against primary source for both; the summaries below are general and may be out of date.

Canada. Canada recognises separate corporate personality and pierces the veil only narrowly. Its federal income tax law contains a statutory general anti-avoidance rule, and the Supreme Court of Canada has interpreted it in a series of cases, beginning with Canada Trustco in 2005 and including Deans Knight in 2023, which asked whether a transaction frustrated the object, spirit and purpose of the provisions relied on. Canada has also legislated changes to its anti-avoidance rule in recent years [unverified — confirm independently]. Canada has extensive related-party and reporting rules.

Guyana. Guyana's company law also rests on separate corporate personality, drawing on the common law tradition [unverified — confirm independently]. Its tax legislation contains provisions aimed at artificial or fictitious transactions, which give the tax authority power to disregard them [unverified — confirm independently]. The scope, wording and case law differ from Canada's and should be confirmed with local counsel and the current statute.

The lesson for a cross-border developer is that the same structure can be tested twice, under two different standards, by two authorities that may share information. Design for the stricter one.

Maintaining personality in practice

A worked example, hypothetical. Your project company owes a supplier 200,000 dollars and cannot pay. The supplier asks a court to hold you personally liable. The court looks at the facts. If the company had its own bank account, paid its own bills, kept minutes of its decisions and dealt with you at arm's length, the supplier's claim against you is weak in most systems. If you paid the company's bills from your personal account one month and took its rent into your account the next, signed contracts in your own name and never held a meeting, the supplier has evidence that the company was not really separate. The rules vary, but the evidence that matters is the same everywhere: separate money, separate decisions, separate paper.

The habit that protects you is dull and daily. Pay company costs from the company account only. Record loans between you and the company in writing. Minute every significant decision. Sign as an officer, with the company's name above your signature.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure whose benefits depend on form alone, with no business activity to support it. The control is to give every entity real substance proportionate to its purpose, and to document why it exists in the structure memorandum.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks that because a structure is legal to form, its benefits are legal to claim. Formation is easy. The test comes when money moves.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught limited liability and piercing the veil. Today's anti-avoidance rules are the tax equivalent: separate personality can be disregarded by a court for liability, and a tax benefit can be denied by an authority for abuse, both on the evidence of how the entity actually behaved.

Recap

Separate legal personality is the foundation, maintained by separate records, money and decisions. Veil piercing, sham and anti-avoidance rules look through form to substance. Related-party dealings must be defensible at arm's length. Canada and Guyana both test structures, under different standards; design for the stricter one.

Professional sign-off required: tax lawyer and corporate lawyer in each jurisdiction.

Next: Nadia, on The Numbers: comparing three structures by the money that actually arrives home.
checklist: Each of my companies has its own bank account, minutes and contracts.
No company's money is mixed with mine or another entity's.
Every entity has substance proportionate to its purpose.
Every related-party payment is set by evidence of market terms.
I can explain each entity's business purpose apart from tax.
I design for the stricter of the jurisdictions my structure touches.
Local counsel has confirmed the anti-avoidance rules in each country.
head: Field checklist
speak: A structure rests on separate legal personality: a company owns its assets, owes its debts and signs its contracts, and its owners are usually liable only for what they invested or guaranteed. That status must be maintained with separate money, minutes, contracts and arm's-length dealings. The law can look through form. Courts can pierce the veil in narrow cases, documents that do not reflect the real deal can be treated as shams, and tax authorities can apply substance over form and general anti-avoidance rules to deny benefits from arrangements that abuse the purpose of the law. Related-party rules require arm's-length prices between my own entities. Canada and Guyana both test structures, with different statutes and case law, which I verify against primary sources. My design principle is that every entity has real substance proportionate to its purpose, and I design for the stricter jurisdiction.
terms: Separate legal personality — the legal rule that a company is a person distinct from its shareholders, owning its own assets and debts.
General anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) — a broad statutory power to deny a tax benefit from arrangements that abuse the purpose of the tax law.
Conduit — an entity that only passes money through without real activity or decision-making of its own.

hostile.q: Your foreign holding company has one nominee director and no office. Why should a tax authority respect it?
hostile.a: On those facts it might not, which is why I would not design it that way. A holding company must have substance proportionate to its purpose: directors who actually decide, board meetings held where it is resident, its own accounts and a business reason beyond the withholding rate, such as holding several projects. If I cannot give it that substance, the benefit is not worth the risk, and I would simplify the structure.

title: Three Structures, One Profit: Counting What Actually Arrives Home
summary: This lesson works one hypothetical project's profit through three structures, step by step, with every rate labelled hypothetical. It then adds running costs and a sale, so the comparison reflects the whole life of the investment rather than one good year.
body:
Compare structures by the dollars that reach you, over the whole life of the asset, after every tax, withholding and running cost. A structure that wins in year one can lose at the sale.

Recall

Q. What is a conduit entity?

A. An entity that only passes money through, without real activity or decisions of its own. Authorities may disregard it under anti-avoidance or treaty anti-abuse rules.

Q. How do you calculate the pessimistic estimate at completion?

A. Actual cost to date plus the remaining budget divided by the cost performance index times the schedule performance index.

Q. What is a preferred return in a waterfall?

A. A return investors receive on their capital before the sponsor shares in profit. The rate is commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, structure advice is often given one year at a time and one tax at a time. Your wealth is built over the whole holding period and taxed at every step. The only fair comparison counts everything, for the whole life. This is an odd-numbered week, so we work forward from inputs to outcome.

The inputs

Hypothetical round numbers. The project earns 1,000,000 dollars of taxable profit a year for five years. At the end of year five it is sold, producing a taxable gain of 6,000,000 dollars. Every rate below is hypothetical, chosen to illustrate the method, not to describe any country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

  • Project-level tax: 25 percent on profit and on the gain.
  • Withholding on dividends to a non-resident: 15 percent paid direct, 5 percent if paid to a qualifying holding company.
  • Personal tax on dividends received: 20 percent.
  • Holding company running cost: 40,000 dollars a year.

Structure A: you own the project company directly

Step 1. Annual profit 1,000,000 dollars, less 25 percent tax of 250,000, leaves 750,000 dollars. Step 2. Dividend to you, a non-resident shareholder, withholding at 15 percent: 112,500 dollars, leaving 637,500 dollars. Step 3. Personal tax at 20 percent on 637,500 dollars is 127,500 dollars, leaving 510,000 dollars a year. Over five years: 2,550,000 dollars.

Step 4. The sale. Gain 6,000,000 dollars, project tax 1,500,000, leaving 4,500,000 dollars. Withholding at 15 percent, 675,000, leaves 3,825,000. Personal tax at 20 percent, 765,000, leaves 3,060,000 dollars. Total to you over the life: 2,550,000 plus 3,060,000, which is 5,610,000 dollars.

Structure B: a qualifying holding company in between

Step 1 is unchanged: 750,000 dollars after project tax. Step 2. Withholding at 5 percent, 37,500, leaves 712,500 dollars in the holding company. Step 3. Running cost 40,000, leaving 672,500. Step 4. Personal tax at 20 percent, 134,500, leaves 538,000 dollars a year. Five years: 2,690,000 dollars.

Step 5. The sale. After project tax, 4,500,000 dollars. Withholding at 5 percent, 225,000, leaves 4,275,000. Personal tax at 20 percent, 855,000, leaves 3,420,000 dollars. Total over the life: 2,690,000 plus 3,420,000, which is 6,110,000 dollars. Structure B delivers 500,000 dollars more than Structure A on these assumptions, after paying 200,000 dollars of running costs.

Say that out loud now.

Count every toll, every year, and the sale; then compare structures by what arrives home.

Structure C: sell the holding company instead of the building

Now a third option that changes only the exit. Suppose, hypothetically, the buyer purchases the shares of the holding company rather than the project assets, and suppose the gain on those shares is taxed once, at 20 percent personally, with no project-level tax. The holding company's share value reflects the building, so assume the share gain is also 6,000,000 dollars. Tax is 1,200,000, leaving 4,800,000 dollars. Annual income is as Structure B, 2,690,000 dollars. Total: 7,490,000 dollars.

That looks best by far, and it is the most dangerous number on the page. A buyer of shares inherits the building's low tax cost, so it pays for the future tax it will bear, usually by lowering the price. Many countries also tax gains on shares that derive their value from local land as if the land itself were sold, which could remove the advantage entirely [unverified — confirm independently]. Structure C is a question for a tax adviser and a buyer, not an assumption for a pro forma.

StructureFive years of incomeSaleTotal
A: direct2,550,0003,060,0005,610,000
B: holding company2,690,0003,420,0006,110,000
C: share sale, if it works2,690,0004,800,0007,490,000

What the comparison does not show

The table ignores timing: money arriving earlier is worth more, so a structure that pays home faster deserves credit, which a net present value comparison captures. It ignores risk: Structure B's 5 percent withholding depends on the holding company qualifying, which depends on substance, and if an authority denied the benefit, the result would fall toward Structure A plus the running costs already spent. And it ignores the other lenses: liability, banking and estate may favour B even if the tax result were equal.

Discounting the comparison

A short worked step, to show what timing does. Discount each structure's cash flows at a hypothetical 8 percent a year. In Structure A, 510,000 dollars a year for five years has a present value of about 2,036,000 dollars, using the five-year annuity factor of about 3.99. The sale proceeds of 3,060,000 dollars in year five, divided by 1.08 to the fifth power, which is about 1.469, are worth about 2,083,000 dollars today. Total about 4,119,000 dollars. In Structure B, 538,000 dollars a year gives about 2,148,000 dollars, and 3,420,000 dollars at year five gives about 2,328,000 dollars, total about 4,476,000 dollars. The gap in today's money is about 357,000 dollars, against 500,000 dollars undiscounted.

The advantage survives but shrinks, because most of it arrives at the sale. Now run the benefit denied case for Structure B: withholding at 15 percent rather than 5 percent, with running costs still paid. Annual income falls to about 478,000 dollars, or 2,390,000 dollars over five years, and sale proceeds fall to about 3,060,000 dollars, for a total of about 5,450,000 dollars undiscounted, which is about 160,000 dollars worse than Structure A. So Structure B is better only if the holding company really qualifies. That single dependency is what the substance work in Week 56 protects.

Reading the result honestly

Put the four results side by side: Structure A at about 5,610,000 dollars, Structure B at about 6,110,000 dollars if the holding company qualifies and about 5,450,000 dollars if it does not, and Structure C as an open question. The honest conclusion is not "Structure B wins by half a million". It is "Structure B wins by about half a million if we can give the holding company real substance, loses by about 160,000 dollars if we cannot, and costs 200,000 dollars of running costs either way". That sentence tells you exactly what to spend money and effort on: the substance of one entity. It also tells your partner what the risk is, in a form they can weigh.

A worked habit: write the result as a range with its condition beside it, every time. A number without its condition invites a decision on the best case. A range with its condition invites the right question, which here is whether the substance can be built and kept.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a structure on its best-case number. The control is to run the comparison with the benefit denied as well as granted, and to choose a structure that still makes sense in the denied case.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares annual income only and adds the exit later. On these numbers the sale carries more than half the total, so the exit decides the structure.

Callback

In Week 11, Nadia taught time value of money and net present value. Discount each structure's cash flows at the same rate before you compare them, and the gap between A and B narrows slightly, because B's advantage is weighted toward the sale in year five.

Recap

Work every structure through the same steps: project tax, withholding, running costs, personal tax, then the sale. Compare totals over the life. Treat a share-sale advantage as a question, not a number, and test every structure with its benefit denied.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each jurisdiction, and an accountant to build the comparison.

Next: Omar, in The Room: presenting a structure chart to a banker and a tax adviser at the same table.
checklist: I compare structures by total after-tax cash over the whole holding period.
Every rate in my comparison is labelled and sourced.
I include running costs for every entity, every year.
I model the sale as carefully as the annual income.
I treat any share-sale advantage as a question for a tax adviser and a buyer.
I run the comparison with the key benefit denied.
I discount each structure's cash flows at the same rate.
head: Field checklist
speak: I compare structures by what arrives home over the whole life. On hypothetical rates, a project earning 1 million a year for five years and sold for a 6 million gain gives about 5.6 million to me if I own it directly, after project tax, 15 percent withholding and personal tax. With a qualifying holding company paying 5 percent withholding and 40 thousand a year to run, I receive about 6.1 million: half a million more after costs. A share sale might show 7.5 million, but that is the most dangerous number on the page, because a buyer of shares prices in the future tax it inherits and many countries tax gains on land-rich shares like land. So I treat it as a question, not an assumption. I also run every structure with the benefit denied, discount the cash flows at the same rate, and remember that the sale often carries more than half the total.
terms: Holding period — the time from buying or building an asset to selling it, over which returns are measured.
Share sale — selling the shares of the company that owns an asset rather than the asset itself.
Benefit denied case — a comparison run on the assumption that a claimed tax benefit is refused.

hostile.q: Your best structure assumes a share sale taxed once. What happens if the buyer will not pay for it?
hostile.a: Then it is Structure B, not C, and I have shown you both. The share sale is a question for the buyer and a tax adviser: a buyer of shares inherits the low tax cost and will usually price that in, and some countries tax gains on land-rich shares as if the land were sold. My base case is the asset sale, and I have also run it with the holding company's withholding benefit denied, so you can see the floor.

title: Presenting the Structure Chart to a Banker and a Tax Adviser at One Table
summary: A banker and a tax adviser read the same structure chart for opposite reasons: one wants security and cash it can reach, the other wants each entity to stand up to an authority. This scene shows how to present one chart to both, the lines to say and never say, and how to keep your advisers working as one team.
body:
Put the banker and the tax adviser in the same room with the same chart. If the structure satisfies both at once, it is designed. If it only satisfies each in a separate meeting, it is two structures pretending to be one.

Recall

Q. In the Day 5 comparison, why is a share-sale result treated as a question rather than a number?

A. Because a buyer of shares inherits the asset's low tax cost and usually prices that in, and some countries tax gains on land-rich shares as if the land were sold.

Q. What is a decision list?

A. The written record at the end of a meeting of each decision, its owner and its date.

Q. What is debt yield?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount. Lenders use it as a sizing limit that does not depend on interest rates or amortisation.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, advisers are usually briefed separately and paid to optimise their own lens. The banker wants to reach cash and assets; the tax adviser may want cash to stay in a layer, or a layer to have independent decision-making that limits what the banker can control. When those wishes collide after closing, you pay to unwind one of them. This meeting catches the collision before it is built.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. You are presenting the structure for a 60-unit apartment building: a project company owning the land and building, owned by a holding company in a second country, owned by you and a partner. The construction loan is 12,000,000 dollars. Around the table: Hana, a credit officer from the lender; Victor, the tax adviser; and your corporate lawyer.

The opening

Say: "One chart, two diagrams. On the left, money: rent comes into the project company, pays operating costs and your interest first, and only then can it pay a dividend up. On the right, control: who appoints the directors and who signs. I want you both to try to break it now, because I would rather redesign it on paper than after closing."

That opening states the structure in the order the banker cares about, invites challenge from both, and sets you as the owner of the whole design rather than the client of either adviser.

The questions, and the question behind each

Hana asks: "If the project defaults, what can I take?" The question behind it is: "Is there anything valuable outside my security?" Answer exactly: "A first mortgage on the land and building, an assignment of rents and contracts, a pledge of the project company's shares by the holding company, and a guarantee as negotiated. Nothing of value sits outside the project company." If something does, say so now.

Victor asks: "Who decides for the holding company, and where?" The question behind it is: "Will this layer have the substance it needs?" Say: "Two directors resident in that country, meeting there quarterly with real agendas, approving dividends and the annual budget." Then turn to Hana: "Does a pledge of the project company's shares by that holding company work for you if its board meets abroad?" You have just made the two advisers solve the collision in front of you.

Hana asks: "Can the holding company take dividends while my loan is outstanding?" Say: "Only from cash left after debt service and reserves, and only if the coverage covenants are met. Victor, does a dividend block cause any problem for the holding company's qualification?" Then stay silent. The answer is the reason you called the meeting.

Say that out loud now.

I own the whole design; I make the advisers solve their collisions in front of me.

Lines never to say

Never say "the tax adviser designed this; I just follow it". It tells the banker no one owns the structure. Never say "that layer is only for tax". It tells the tax adviser, and later an authority, that the layer has no other purpose. Never promise the banker cash sweeps that the tax adviser has told you would break the holding company's qualification. If you do not know, say "I will confirm by Friday, with both of you copied."

Holding your state

When two advisers disagree in front of you, you may feel caught between experts. Do not pick a side quickly. Restate each position in one sentence, then ask what each would need to accept the other's requirement. A worked example: Hana wants a cash sweep of all excess cash; Victor wants the holding company to approve distributions itself. Restated, the compromise is a cash trap only on covenant breach, with ordinary distributions approved by the holding company's board. You did not decide the expert question; you designed the question so the experts could answer it.

Working with advisers

This month's thread is working with advisers. Every adviser sees the problem through the lens they are paid for, and most are honest about it. Your job is not to know more than they do in their field. It is to make sure every adviser sees the whole design, to ask each "what facts would change your view?", and to put their advice in writing against the same version of the structure memorandum. Conflicting advice in separate emails is a liability; conflicting advice resolved in one meeting, minuted, is an asset.

Brief advisers with facts, not conclusions. "Can you make this work?" invites a yes. "Here are the facts; what would you recommend and what would worry you?" invites judgment. Pay for that judgment, and keep a short note after every adviser meeting of what was decided and what is still open. Advisers change; your notes stay.

The close

A worked close: "Decisions. One: the share pledge stands, and Victor confirms in writing by Friday that it does not affect qualification. Two: distributions only after debt service and reserves, with a cash trap on covenant breach. Three: the holding company's board calendar is fixed for the year. Four: I circulate the revised memorandum on Monday to all three of you." Then stop talking.

The question behind the meeting

Behind every question Hana and Victor ask is one shared question: does this owner understand his own structure? A banker lends partly against the building and partly against the borrower's judgment. A tax adviser's advice is only as good as the facts the client actually lives by. If you can explain each entity's purpose, its substance and its effect on security in plain sentences, both of them leave with confidence in you as well as in the chart. If you defer every question to the other adviser, they both leave with doubts, and the doubts show up later as tighter terms and higher fees.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is closing the loan on terms that quietly break the tax design, or the reverse. The control is one memorandum, one meeting with both advisers, and written confirmation from each against the same version.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner shows the banker a simplified chart that omits the holding layer, to avoid questions. The banker finds it in diligence, and now the question is about you, not the structure.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught engagement letters and how to challenge advice. Today you used both: each adviser is engaged on the whole memorandum, and the question "what would worry you?" is a way to challenge without accusing.

Recap

Present one chart to both advisers. Answer the banker on security exactly, the tax adviser on substance exactly, and make them resolve collisions in front of you. Never disown the design or describe a layer as only for tax. Close with written confirmations against one version.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions, a Red Pen drill on a structure memorandum and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I present one structure chart to the banker and the tax adviser together.
I can state the lender's full security package exactly.
I can state who decides for each entity and where.
I never describe a layer as existing only for tax.
I ask advisers what facts would change their view.
Every adviser confirms in writing against the same memorandum version.
I keep a note after each adviser meeting of what was decided and what is open.
head: Field checklist
speak: I put the banker and the tax adviser in one room with one chart, because a structure that only satisfies each separately is two structures. I open with the money, in the order the banker cares about: rent in, operating costs and interest first, then dividends up. Then control: who appoints and who signs. I invite both to break it. When the banker asks what she can take, I state the security exactly. When the tax adviser asks who decides for the holding company, I name the directors and where they meet, then ask the banker whether that works for her share pledge, so they solve the collision in front of me. I never say a layer is only for tax, and I never disown the design. When they disagree, I restate each position and ask what each needs. I close with written confirmations from both against the same memorandum version.
terms: Share pledge — security over the shares of a company, letting the lender take control of the company on default.
Cash trap — a loan term that stops distributions and holds cash in the borrower when a covenant is breached.
Qualification — meeting the conditions a tax benefit requires, such as a holding company's residence and substance.

hostile.q: Your tax adviser says the holding company must decide its own dividends abroad. How do I know cash will not leave before my loan is paid?
hostile.a: Because the loan agreement controls the project company, where the cash is earned. No dividend can leave it until debt service and reserves are paid and the coverage covenants are met, and on a breach cash is trapped. The holding company's board approves dividends only from what the project company is permitted to pay. You also hold a pledge of the project company's shares. The tax adviser has confirmed in writing that these terms do not affect qualification.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 55 Review: Structure as Design
summary: This review tests the week's core ideas: the six lenses as design loads, the two diagrams, sequencing, leakage, the law that tests a structure and how to present one to advisers. It ends with a Red Pen drill on a structure memorandum and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: design a structure from six loads, draw the money and the control on one page each, give every entity a purpose and real substance, and count what arrives home over the whole life.

Recall

Q. What is a cash trap?

A. A loan term that stops distributions and holds cash in the borrower when a covenant is breached.

Q. What is Rule 54?

A. No change to structure, use or loads goes ahead without the engineer of record's written approval in the change log, and a structural warning means evacuate first and meet second.

Q. What is a refinance take-out?

A. A permanent loan that repays the construction loan once the building is complete and stabilised.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the rest of this phase builds on today's method. Residence, treaties, repatriation and exit are all lenses on the same structure chart. If you can answer these six questions without notes, the next nine weeks have a frame to hang on. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the six lenses and what each asks.

Answer: Tax: what each layer pays and leaks. Liability: what a claim can reach. Banking: whether a lender can take clean security and accounts can run. Governance: who decides and signs. Estate: what happens on death or incapacity. Exit: how the asset can be sold, refinanced or passed on.

Question 2. What two diagrams does every structure need, and why both?

Answer: A flow-of-funds diagram and a flow-of-control diagram. Money and control often follow different paths, and where they differ is where disputes and tax challenges arise.

Question 3. Why is sequencing part of the design?

Answer: Because land signed in the wrong name, investors admitted before the agreement or accounts opened on the wrong mandate can each create tax, liability or governance problems that are expensive or impossible to undo.

Question 4. What are the four kinds of leakage?

Answer: Project-level tax, withholding on payments to non-residents, tax at holding layers, and friction, the yearly running cost of each entity.

Question 5. What is a general anti-avoidance rule?

Answer: A broad statutory power, found in many tax systems, to deny a tax benefit from arrangements that abuse the purpose of the law. Tests differ by country; verify them against the primary source.

Question 6. What did Enron teach you?

Answer: Rule 55: every entity has a one-sentence business purpose, every related-party arrangement is disclosed and independently priced, and the whole structure is drawn on one page for any lender or investor before they commit.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Omar framed structure as design from six loads, drawn twice and built in sequence. Ford and Cole took Enron, where structure was designed to hide rather than carry, giving Rule 55. Warrick measured leakage layer by layer. Omar taught separate legal personality and the doctrines that look through it, with a comparison of Canada and Guyana. Nadia compared three structures over a whole holding period. Omar ran the room with a banker and a tax adviser at one table.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical structure memorandum and find the defects before reading on.

Structure Memorandum, Project North. The land was purchased by the Sponsor personally last month and will be transferred to ProjectCo after the loan closes. ProjectCo is owned by HoldCo A, which exists for tax purposes. HoldCo A's sole director is a corporate services provider that signs on instruction from the Sponsor. ManageCo, owned by the Sponsor, will charge ProjectCo a development fee of 9 percent of total cost. Investors will subscribe for shares in ProjectCo this month; the shareholder agreement will follow. Projected leakage is 18 percent, based on annual income in a stabilised year. The lender has been shown a simplified chart.

The defects. First, the land was bought personally and will be moved later, a sequencing error that can trigger transfer tax twice and a taxable disposition; it also leaves the lender without clean security at closing. Second, HoldCo A "exists for tax purposes", a stated purpose that invites anti-avoidance challenge and fails Rule 55. Third, its sole director signs on instruction, so it has no substance and looks like a conduit. Fourth, the development fee is set by the sponsor on both sides with no market evidence, an undisclosed related-party pricing issue. Fifth, investors are admitted before the shareholder agreement exists. Sixth, leakage is measured on one stabilised year only, ignoring sale and death. Seventh, the lender was shown a simplified chart, the Enron error on a small scale.

A second worked check. Fix each defect in one line: buy the land in ProjectCo from the start; give HoldCo A a business purpose and directors who decide; price the fee from market evidence and disclose it; sign the shareholder agreement before subscription; build the leakage table for income, sale and death; show the lender the full chart.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why can't we just form a company and get started?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "We can, and we should keep it as simple as the job allows. But the structure has to carry six things at once: tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit. So before we form anything, I draw two pictures on one page each: where the money goes and where it is taxed, and who controls and signs. Then I decide the order: the company buys the land, the agreement is signed before anyone invests, the accounts open on the right authority. Every entity needs a one-sentence purpose beyond tax and real substance, because authorities can look through form. I measure what reaches us after every layer, for income, a sale and a death, and I show the lender the full chart. That is a few days of work now against years of unwinding later."

Score your answer. Did you lead with a decision? Did you name the six lenses? Did you mention sequencing with an example? Did you finish inside two minutes?

Using the Red Pen on your own documents

The planted defects above are the most common ones in real structure memoranda, and each comes from the same habit: writing the memo after decisions have been made, to describe them, rather than before, to test them. Before your next project, write the memorandum first. Then run the Red Pen on it yourself, line by line, asking of each sentence: is this a fact or a hope, does it say why, and would I be comfortable if a lender, an investor and a tax auditor read it on the same day? Any sentence that fails one of those three tests is a defect you have found for free.

A worked example: the line "the shareholder agreement will follow" is a hope, it does not say why, and an investor reading it would ask what terms they are subscribing on. Rewrite it as a sequencing step with a date, and the defect becomes a task.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is accepting structure advice one lens at a time. The control is one memorandum, every adviser reading it, and you owning the design.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising the six lenses as a list instead of testing every entity against them. The list is easy; the test is the skill.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the project charter: purpose, authorities and reporting written down before work starts. The structure memorandum is a charter for the ownership itself, and it fails the same way a charter does: by being written once and never read again.

Recap

Six lenses, two diagrams, sequencing, leakage over the whole life, substance behind form, and one memorandum every adviser reads. Rule 55 keeps every entity purposeful, disclosed and drawable on one page.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, structure became design. A structure carries six loads: tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit. I draw it twice, money and control, each on one page. I sequence it so the company buys the land, the agreement is signed before anyone invests and accounts open on the right authority. Every entity needs a one-sentence purpose beyond tax and real substance, because separate legal personality can be looked through by courts and tax authorities using anti-avoidance rules. I measure leakage, meaning project tax, withholding, holding-layer tax and running costs, over the whole holding period, including a sale and a death, and I test the structure with its main benefit denied. I present one chart to the banker and the tax adviser together and make them resolve collisions in front of me. Rule 55, from Enron: purpose, disclosure and one page shown in full.
terms: Structure memorandum — a short document holding a structure's diagrams, each entity's purpose and the sequencing plan.
Red Pen drill — reading a short document to find planted defects before they are revealed.
Boardroom drill — explaining a week's subject in two minutes as if to a partner, then comparing with a model answer.

hostile.q: Your memorandum says the holding company exists for tax purposes. Why should I, as your lender, not worry about that?
hostile.a: You should, and that line was wrong. The holding company's purpose is to hold my interests in several projects and to separate them from my personal estate, and it has directors who meet and decide in its country of residence. I have rewritten the memorandum to say so, and I will show you the full chart, the security you take and the tax adviser's written confirmation that the loan terms do not affect it.
